newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG drops firearm charges against British mercenary.
newsitem.headline: PNG drops firearm charges against British mercenary.

text.p: Illegal firearm charges against British mercenary leader Tim Spicer, who led an aborted mission to Papua New Guinea last month, have been dropped, a prosecution official said on Tuesday.
"On the advise of the public prosecutor the charges were dropped," Chief of Police Prosecution Wee Kati told Reuters just before the scheduled start of Spicer's trial.
Spicer, a retired British colonel who led 70 African mercenaries to the South Pacific nation, had pleaded not guilty to illegally possessing a Russian pistol and ammunition.
Kati said there were legal problems with the manner in which Spicer's Port Moresby flat was searched and the pistol seized before he was charged.

Spicer's US$36 million mission sparked the worst political crisis in Papua New Guinea since independence in 1975, with the army revolting and forcing the prime minister Sir Julius Chan to step aside pending an inquiry into the mercenary deal.

Rebel army officers threw the foreign soldiers out of the country, but detained Spicer, eventually handing him over to police to be charged with illegally possessing a firearm. Spicer, 44, was expected to leave Papua New Guinea after concluding his evidence to the mercenary inquiry on Tuesday.
